title: Tell your AI about you
outcome: Your assistant (Claude or ChatGPT) remembers who you are, whether you sell software or services, your ideal customer, territory, competitors and proof point, and applies the library's data rules to every later answer.
when: At the start of a new chat, before any other prompt in this library. If you use Claude or ChatGPT Projects, the Project version is the better path: you set it once.
roles: Account Executive, SDR / BDR, Account & Customer Success Manager, Sales Leader & RevOps, Marketing & ABM, Presales & Solutions, Services, SI & Staffing Seller, Partnerships & Alliances
quick_prompt: Remember for this chat: I'm [My role]; I sell [I sell]: [What I sell] to [Ideal customer] in [Territory]; competitors [Competitors]; customers [Our customers]. Confirm in 6 lines and use these defaults.
detailed_prompt:
You are my sales research partner for this chat. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

ABOUT ME (edit these)
- My role: [e.g. Enterprise AE, North America retail]
- I sell: [software, services or both, e.g. services]
- What I sell: [e.g. cloud data-platform migration plus managed data engineering]
- Typical deal: [e.g. $250K–$1.5M, 6–9 months]
- Ideal customer: [e.g. Retail, 5,000+ employees, $1B+ revenue]
- Buyers: [e.g. CIO, Chief Data Officer; the CIO signs]
- Territory: [e.g. United States of America; target.com, kroger.com]
- Competitors: [companies or products, e.g. Accenture, Google BigQuery]
- Our customers: [e.g. Contoso Retail, Fabrikam Foods]
- Focus: [e.g. displacing incumbents]
- Proof point: [e.g. Contoso Retail closes its books two days faster]
- Answer format: [e.g. tables first, under 400 words]

STEPS (now)
1. Find each competitor and customer in Draup. Use the exact match; ask only if there is none or several. Record a product competitor with its maker.
2. Map What I sell to Draup business functions and workloads, dropping any that don't fit.

OUTPUT (now)
- 6 lines: me and what I sell; customer and buyers; territory; competitors (product → maker) and customers as Draup names; focus and proof point; format.
- The mapped workloads, then "Ready. Name an account."

RULES (every later answer; leave as is)
- Fill prompt inputs from ABOUT ME unless I override them; ask if one is missing.
- Use Draup for every fact; label outside knowledge. Date every number. Write "Not in Draup" for gaps; never guess. Label inferences "likely".
- Companies: find by website, confirm the parent, flag subsidiaries; resolve each name before listing. Retry an empty name once with Draup's spelling ("Accenture", not "Accenture plc"; "United States of America"; "Life Sciences"; business functions such as "IT" or "Supply Chain").
- When I've named competitors, check each account's whole stack for their products before writing why-this-matters.
- Narrow pulls by function or workload; show the top 10 first, then offer more.
- Executives: full profile title, not the seniority label (in banking and consulting VP and SVP are mid-level); 10 per page, 3 pages max; if Europe or the UK returns none, rerun without location; professional information only. Moves: about 10 latest per type, so narrow by workload.
- Money: annual, millions of reporting currency, fiscal years (can run ahead of the calendar); latest regional split only; check divestments before calling a drop over 5% a cut. IT and R&D spend are Draup estimates that often track revenue. Forecasts over 15% off the latest actual are model estimates.
- Tech: trust last-seen date and usage strength; ignore first-seen dates and "Generic" rows; say "fading", not "dropped". Ignore an account's own products if it sells technology.
- Hiring and news cover 12 months. Postings are openings, not hires; skip partial first and last months. Drop news noise (outages, stock chatter, charity, look-alikes, re-dated stories); the account must be the actor.
- Engagements and outsourced headcount are Draup estimates, not contracts. Priority tools and providers are "linked", not confirmed.
- Never use Draup's own customer or user data. End every answer with "Recommended next step" and "Gaps".

Confirm the 6-line summary, then apply ABOUT ME and the RULES to everything I ask in this chat.
followups: Change my focus to expanding existing customers and confirm. || Add Infosys and Databricks to my competitors and give their Draup names and makers. || Run the one-page account brief on the first named account in my territory.
tips: Fill in "I sell": several prompts read a partner as a co-sell ally for software sellers but as an incumbent to displace for services sellers. || List competitors as products when that is how you meet them (for example a cloud data platform). Claude records the maker so it can spot them in an account's tech stack. || Use company websites and full country names; they match Draup most reliably.

title: One-page account brief
outcome: A one-page brief on size, money, priorities, recent deals and any competitor in the stack, ending with who to call and why now.
when: An account just landed on your list, or before a first meeting.
roles: Account Executive, Presales & Solutions, Account & Customer Success Manager, SDR / BDR
quick_prompt: One-page Draup brief on [Company]: size, latest revenue and IT spend with growth, the 8 priorities closest to [What I sell], acquisitions in 3 years, and who to call first. Date every number.
detailed_prompt:
Act as my sales research analyst. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. siemens.com]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. cloud data-platform modernisation services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]
- Competitor: [optional company or product, e.g. Snowflake]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] by website and confirm it is the parent, not a subsidiary, brand or sister company; if unsure, ask me. Use Draup's exact name from then on.
2. Pull the profile; latest fiscal-year revenue, EBITDA, IT and R&D spend with year-on-year growth and next-year forecast; and revenue by business unit and region. If private, show funding instead.
3. Pull stated priorities and keep the 8 most relevant to [What I sell], newest first.
4. Pull acquisitions from the last 3 years.
5. If I named a competitor, check the whole tech stack for its products, in any area; if it is a services firm, check its outsourcing engagements at the account instead (Draup estimates, not contracts).

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the answer and what it means for [What I sell].
- "The numbers": Metric | Latest FY | YoY | Next-year forecast; then business units and regions with % share.
- "What they're focused on": Priority | Function | Source + quarter | Likely owner (title). Up to 8.
- "Recent deals": Date | Company acquired | Size or "undisclosed" | Why they bought it. Flag divestments and duplicates.
- "Competitor in the stack" (if named): Product | Maker | Usage strength | Last seen.
- "Why this matters for [What I sell]": 3 bullets: fact → implication → action.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title or name), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting) and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- If [Company] sells technology, drop priorities about its own products and its own products from linked tools.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- Pull company lists 10 rows at a time and priorities 10 at a time; show the top results first and offer to continue.
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill gaps from memory.
- If a forecast is more than 15% from the latest actual, or contradicts the latest year-on-year change, show both and call it a model estimate.
- The acquisitions table can be incomplete: if it is thin but priorities or news name an acquired company, check 12 months of M&A news and say so. Divestments come from news only.
- Use the latest year's regional split only. Check for a divestment or restatement before calling a drop over 5% a cut.
- Keep to about 400 words plus tables. Show the top results first, then offer to continue rather than pulling everything.
followups: Now map the buying committee for [Business function]. || Which of these priorities have the most hiring behind them? || Is their budget growing or shrinking? Show the 3-year trend. || Turn the 'Why this matters' section into a 90-word email to the person in the next step.
tips: Use the company website rather than the name; it is the most reliable way to land on the right company. || Add your main competitor: finding it, or its absence, in the stack is often the most useful line in the brief. || Fiscal years and quarters follow the company's own calendar and can run ahead of the calendar year.

title: 10-minute pre-call snapshot
outcome: Five short bullets you can read in the lobby: who they are, what just happened, where hiring is rising, the priority closest to your offer, and one question to ask.
when: You have a call in 10 minutes and no time for a full brief.
roles: Account Executive, SDR / BDR, Account & Customer Success Manager, Presales & Solutions
data: Company & financials, News signals, Hiring & job postings, Priorities & opportunities
quick_prompt: Call with [Company] in 10 minutes. Five bullets, 25 words each: what they do and size; 2 events from the last 90 days; top 3 workloads trending up; the priority closest to [What I sell]; one question.
detailed_prompt:
Act as my pre-call research assistant. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. siemens.com]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. industrial AI and edge-cloud integration services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]
- Meeting with: [optional title, e.g. VP Digital Industries IT]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] by website and confirm it is the parent, not a subsidiary, brand or sister company; if unsure, ask me. Use Draup's exact name from then on.
2. Pull the profile: what they do, workforce, latest revenue and its fiscal year.
3. Pull the top news from the last 90 days where [Company] is the actor.
4. Pull the top 3 workloads trending up in hiring (12 months), by postings; if fewer than 3 are rising, show those and say so.
5. Pull stated priorities and pick the one closest to [What I sell], preferring the function of the person I'm meeting.

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the answer and what it means for [What I sell].
- 0. If I named who I'm meeting: one priority they likely own, and their time in role if the title is on the first executives page for that function.
- Then exactly 5 bullets, 25 words or fewer each:
  1. What they do and their size (workforce, revenue, fiscal year).
  2. The 2 most important events from the last 90 days, each dated.
  3. The top 3 workloads trending up, with posting counts.
  4. The priority closest to [What I sell], with source and quarter.
  5. One open question that cites a fact from bullets 1–4.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title or name), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting) and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- If fewer than 2 real events exist, say so; don't pad.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- Pull company lists 10 rows at a time and priorities 10 at a time; show the top results first and offer to continue.
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill gaps from memory.
- Drop news noise: outages (unless I sell security), stock chatter, charity, awards, passing mentions, look-alike or sister companies, and re-dated old stories (use the event date in the text). Give source, headline and link if Draup has one.
- Postings are openings, not hires. Ignore the first and last months of a monthly series; they are usually partial.
- Keep to about 180 words plus tables. Show the top results first, then offer to continue rather than pulling everything.
followups: Give me 3 more questions like bullet 5, each tied to a different fact. || Who else from [Company] should be in the next meeting? || Expand bullet 2: what changed and why it matters for [What I sell].
tips: Name who you're meeting. Claude picks the priority in their function instead of the company-wide top one. || If you have 30 minutes rather than 10, run the one-page account brief instead.

title: Is their budget growing or shrinking?
outcome: A verdict on whether the account's budget is growing, holding or shrinking, the IT spend split, and the deal size and pitch that fit.
when: Before you set deal size or pick a value story, or when a champion says 'budgets are tight'.
roles: Account Executive, Account & Customer Success Manager, Sales Leader & RevOps, Services, SI & Staffing Seller
quick_prompt: Is [Company]'s budget growing, holding or shrinking? 3-year revenue, EBITDA, IT and R&D spend plus forecast, the IT spend split, a verdict with evidence, deal-size implication and pitch for [What I sell].
detailed_prompt:
Act as my sales finance analyst. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. unilever.com]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. managed data engineering and analytics services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] by website and confirm it is the parent, not a subsidiary, brand or sister company; if unsure, ask me. Use Draup's exact name from then on.
2. Pull revenue, EBITDA, IT and R&D spend for the last 3 fiscal years, plus Draup's next-year forecast.
3. Pull the IT spend split for the latest and prior year.
4. Pull acquisitions (3 years), and divestments, layoffs and cost programmes from news (12 months; say so).

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the answer and what it means for [What I sell].
- "3-year trend": Fiscal year | Revenue | YoY | EBITDA margin | IT spend | YoY | R&D | YoY, forecast year last.
- Verdict: Growing, Holding or Shrinking, with 3 dated evidence bullets.
- "IT spend split (Draup estimate)": Category | Latest FY | Prior FY | YoY | % of total.
- "Deal-size implication": one line on how big a first deal to propose.
- "What to pitch": 3 bullets fitting the verdict, naming the IT spend category most addressable by [What I sell] and its likely owner (title).
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title or name), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting) and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Verdict (editable default): Growing = revenue and EBITDA up over 3% a year; Shrinking = either down over 5% after the divestment check; else Holding.
- For any drop over 5%, name the divestment, demerger or restatement behind it, or say none falls in that year.
- If every IT split category moves with the total, call the split proportional.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill gaps from memory.
- IT and R&D spend are Draup estimates, and IT spend often moves with revenue; don't treat IT-spend growth as a separate signal.
- If a forecast is more than 15% from the latest actual, or contradicts the latest year-on-year change, show both and call it a model estimate.
- Financials are annual, in millions of reporting currency, by fiscal year (which can run ahead of the calendar).
- Keep to about 350 words plus tables. Show the top results first, then offer to continue rather than pulling everything.
followups: Convert everything to USD and compare with [Company 2]. || Which business units are growing fastest? || Draft a cost-takeout talk track for the CFO based on this.
tips: A falling number is not always a cut. Spin-offs and restatements often explain big drops; the prompt checks for them. || The IT spend split is Draup's estimate. Use it to size the conversation, not as a reported figure.

title: Which priority to anchor your pitch on
outcome: Where the account's priorities cluster, how each fits what you sell, and the single priority to lead with, with its likely owner and linked vendors.
when: You need to know which initiative to anchor a pitch on.
roles: Account Executive, Presales & Solutions, Account & Customer Success Manager, Services, SI & Staffing Seller
quick_prompt: Rank the top 5 workloads in [Company]'s priorities by fit to [What I sell], then list the top 8 priorities in the best-fit function with source, quarter, likely owner and linked providers. Name one anchor.
detailed_prompt:
Act as my sales strategy analyst. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. siemens.com]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. cloud data-platform modernisation services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]
- Business function: [optional, e.g. IT; leave blank and Claude picks]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] by website and confirm it is the parent, not a subsidiary, brand or sister company; if unsure, ask me. Use Draup's exact name from then on.
2. Pull how many priorities mention each workload. Mark each Strong, Partial or No fit to [What I sell] and keep the top 5 by fit, then count.
3. If I gave no business function, choose the one holding most Strong-fit workloads and say why.
4. Pull up to 8 priorities for that function and sort them by date yourself, newest first.

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the answer and what it means for [What I sell].
- "Where priorities cluster": Rank | Workload | # priorities | Fit | Reason (5 words or fewer). Top 5.
- "Top priorities in [Business function]": Priority | One-line summary | Source (earnings call or news) + quarter | Workloads | Likely owner (title) | Up to 3 linked providers.
- "Best anchor for [What I sell]": the one priority to lead with and 2 bullets on why.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title or name), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting) and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Leave out linked technology or use cases that clearly don't fit the industry.
- In the provider column, leave out the company's own subsidiaries, recruiters, staffing firms, agencies and market-research firms.
- If the function has no priorities, say so and show the 3 nearest functions by priority count.
- If [Company] sells technology, drop priorities about its own products and its own products from linked tools.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- Pull company lists 10 rows at a time and priorities 10 at a time; show the top results first and offer to continue.
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill gaps from memory.
- Tools and providers are linked to priorities by workload, not confirmed: say "linked", never "used for". Quarter labels are fiscal and can run ahead of the calendar.
- Label anything you infer (buyer role, intent, fit, integration work) as "likely".
- Keep to about 350 words plus tables. Show the top results first, then offer to continue rather than pulling everything.
followups: For the anchor priority, which technology and incumbent vendors are linked? || Who owns the anchor priority? Find executives tagged to its workloads. || Is there hiring behind these priorities, or are they just talk?
tips: Leaving the function blank lets Claude choose where your offer fits best. || Priorities from earnings calls often carry more weight than ones inferred from news.

title: Their leaders' own words on [Topic]
outcome: Up to six verbatim quotes from leadership on your topic, with speaker, fiscal quarter and call date, or the annual-filing sections to read when there's no call.
when: You want to open with the customer's own words rather than your claims.
roles: Account Executive, Presales & Solutions, Marketing & ABM, Account & Customer Success Manager
quick_prompt: Quote [Company]'s leaders on [Topic] from the latest earnings call: up to 6 verbatim quotes with speaker, title, fiscal quarter and call date. If there's no call, list annual filings and sections to read.
detailed_prompt:
Act as my sales research analyst. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. target.com]
- Topic: [e.g. AI, supply chain, technology investment]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. AI-driven demand forecasting software — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] by website and confirm it is the parent, not a subsidiary, brand or sister company; if unsure, ask me. Use Draup's exact name from then on.
2. List the earnings-call transcripts, newest first, and open the most recent. Note each speaker's title from the introductions, and whether it is an analyst or a press call.
3. Find every passage where an executive talks about [Topic], preferring the CEO and CFO. If [Topic] isn't there, say so and repeat on the previous call.
4. Fallback: if there are no transcripts, or neither call mentions [Topic], pull the annual filings Draup holds for the last 5 years (US SEC filers only).

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the answer and what it means for [What I sell].
- Header: call date, the company's own name for the period with Draup's label in brackets, call type.
- "Quotes": # | Speaker | Title | Verbatim quote (40 words or fewer) | What it signals. Up to 6, strongest first.
- "How to use this with [What I sell]": 2 bullets, each pairing a quote with a talking point.
- Fallback only, "Filings to read": Fiscal year | Type | Filed date | Link; then up to 4 sections for [What I sell] (e.g. Risk Factors, Management's Discussion and Analysis, Business, Properties), one line each on what to look for.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title or name), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting) and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Quote word for word; trim with an ellipsis, never paraphrase inside quotation marks. Executives only, not analysts.
- Don't summarise or quote a filing you haven't opened. Non-US companies usually have none; that's expected.
- Read only what you need; reproduce nothing beyond the quotes.
- Draup's quarter label follows the fiscal year and can run ahead of the company's own wording; show both.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill gaps from memory.
- Keep to about 300 words plus tables. Show the top results first, then offer to continue rather than pulling everything.
followups: Do the same for the previous call. Has the tone on [Topic] changed? || Pull every number they stated in this call into a table. || Write a 3-line email opener using the strongest quote.
tips: Quarters follow the company's fiscal year, which can run a year ahead of the calendar. The prompt shows both labels. || For US-listed companies, the filing fallback points you to risk-factor language you can cite.

title: Numbers from the latest call
outcome: Every number management stated on the latest earnings call (guidance, targets, KPIs, investment plans) in one table, with the three that matter for your deal and the question each opens.
when: Building a business case, a QBR, or an executive email that should use their numbers, not yours.
roles: Account Executive, Account & Customer Success Manager, Presales & Solutions, Sales Leader & RevOps
quick_prompt: Put every number management stated on [Company]'s latest earnings call in a table: metric, value, period, actual or guidance, speaker, short quote. Then the 3 that matter for [What I sell], each with a question to ask.
detailed_prompt:
Act as my financial analyst for a sales team. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. target.com]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. store and supply-chain technology modernisation — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] by website and confirm it is the parent, not a subsidiary, brand or sister company; if unsure, ask me. Use Draup's exact name from then on.
2. List the earnings-call transcripts, newest first, and open the most recent analyst call. If the newest is a press call, use the latest analyst call and say so.
3. Note each executive's title from the introductions.
4. Extract every number an executive states: results, guidance, targets, capital spending, technology investment, store or site counts, headcount, AI or digital metrics, savings programmes.

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the answer and what it means for [What I sell].
- Header: call date, the company's own name for the period, Draup's quarter label in brackets.
- "What they said", grouped as Guidance / Investment and capex / Operating KPIs / Technology, AI and digital: Metric | Value | Period it refers to | Actual, guidance or target | Raised, lowered or new (only if said) | Speaker | Quote (20 words or fewer). Up to 25 rows.
- "Numbers that matter for [What I sell]": 3 bullets, each a number, the conversation it opens and the question to ask.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title or name), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting) and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Executives only; skip numbers that appear only in analysts' questions.
- Keep units and currency as stated ("$5 billion to $6 billion", "about 6%"). Don't round or convert unless I ask.
- Separate the period a number refers to from the call's quarter. Mark raised or lowered only if the speaker compares with earlier guidance.
- Draup's quarter label follows the fiscal year and can run ahead of the company's wording; show both.
- No transcript: say so and suggest the filing fallback in the leaders' own words prompt.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)

detailed_prompt:
Act as my sales operations analyst building a target account list. Use Draup for Sales for every fact.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Vertical: [Industry, e.g. Banking & Financial Services]
- Country: [HQ country in full, e.g. India]
- Minimum employees: [e.g. 5,000]
- Technology (optional): [Product they must run, e.g. SAP S/4HANA]
- Rank by: [revenue, workforce or Opportunity Index; default revenue]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. core-banking modernisation services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]

STEPS
1. Resolve the vertical, country and technology to Draup's names.
2. List companies with primary vertical [Vertical], HQ in [Country] and, if given, [Technology] in their tech stack (that filter is the evidence). Leave the size minimum off; sort by [Rank by].
3. Apply [Minimum employees] yourself: count matches, companies lacking a workforce figure, and matches by band: [Minimum]–9,999 (skip if empty), 10,000–49,999, 50,000+.
4. For the 5 best fits only, pull 90-day top news and confirm [Technology] with its last-seen date.

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — how big the list is and what it means for [What I sell].
- Header: "N companies match" (or "250+"), band counts, and "M more lack a workforce figure; include them?"
- Top 25 (by [Rank by]): Rank | Company | Workforce | Revenue ($M, FY) | IT spend ($M, FY) | Opportunity Index | Service providers (3, unranked) | Postings (90 days) | Who to call (likely title) | Flag.
- "Where to start" (5 rows): Company | Why it fits | Why now (freshest material dated event, or "none in 90 days") | [Technology] last seen.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting), and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Flag "check vertical" if a description doesn't fit.
- IT spend is a Draup estimate, often modelled from revenue: label it "Draup-estimated"; its growth is not a separate signal.

- Flag "check revenue" when revenue per employee is above $5M (often gross trading revenue). (editable default)
STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- Pull company lists 10 rows at a time and priorities 10 at a time; show the top results first and offer to continue.
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill from memory.

- Pull 10 companies per page (each row is large), at most 3 pages. For the total, check whether a 250th match exists and report "250+" if it does; size-band and missing-workforce counts then cover the rows pulled.
- Show USD millions using Draup's conversion rate; if Draup gives none, name the rate and date and mark it as outside Draup.
- Keep to about 450 words plus tables. Show the top results first, then offer to continue rather than pulling everything.

- Country: [In full, e.g. United States of America]
- Window: [default last 12 months]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. data-platform migration services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]

STEPS
1. Resolve the technology (or role) and country to Draup's names; show them.

- "Industries": Industry | Postings | Share %, plus top titles.
- "Removed": name and why.
- Recommended next step: who to contact (title), what to do (call, email, intro, meeting), and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Label tables with country, window and filter (product or keyword).
- "Who to call" = likely buyer title for [What I sell] at that company's size.

title: Tier my accounts by propensity to buy

3. For the 10 highest-Fit accounts, count distinct dated news events (90 days) with the company as actor. Others: "not checked", scored 10.
4. Score, add up and tier.

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — the A accounts and what they share.
- Table: Tier | Account | Fit | Timing | Total | Grid | Strongest driver | Weakest driver. By total.

- Recommended next step: who to contact (title), what to do, and why now (one dated fact).
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Rubric (editable defaults). FIT 50: revenue in band 15 (within 2x 8, else 3); revenue growth 10 (over 5% 10, 0–5% 6, −5–0% 3, else 0); Opportunity Index 15 (score ÷ 10 × 15); industry 5 (in target 5, else 0; all 5 if blank); IT spend 5 (over $500M 5, $100–500M 3, else 1), light as it is modelled from revenue. TIMING 50: news events 20 (0 = 0, 1–2 = 8, 3–5 = 14, 6+ = 20); hiring % 15 (over 10% 15, 5–10% 10, 2–5% 5, else 0); workforce growth 15 (over 3% 15, 0–3% 10, −3–0% 5, else 0).
- Missing value = half that item's points, flagged. Ignore yes/no signal flags.
- Tiers: A 70+, B 50–69, C under 50. Grid: Fit 30+ and Timing 25+ = Pursue now; Fit only = Nurture; Timing only = Opportunistic; neither = Deprioritise.
- For news, skip stock chatter, awards, passing mentions and look-alikes.

quick_prompt: Compare [Company]'s Draup employer-value scores with [Hiring rivals]: overall index, reviews analysed, pillar scores, the 3 weakest pillars with review themes, and RPO angles for [What I sell].
detailed_prompt:
Act as my talent-acquisition services strategist. Use the Draup for Talent connector for employer-value scores, and the Draup for Sales connector for company lookups. Don't use outside knowledge unless I ask, and label it if you do.

INPUTS (edit these)
- Company: [website, e.g. walmart.com]
- Hiring rivals: [up to 3 companies it competes with for hires, e.g. amazon.com, target.com]
- Location (optional): [country or metro for location-level scores, e.g. India]
- What I sell: [one line, e.g. RPO and employer-branding services — skip if you ran the start-here prompt]

STEPS
1. Find [Company] and each rival by website and confirm the parent company. Tell me if a rival can't be found and carry on.
2. For each, pull the employer-value scores: overall index, employee reviews analysed, and every pillar and sub-pillar score. Use [Location] scores if given; otherwise company-wide.
3. Find [Company]'s 3 weakest pillars: the lowest scores and the biggest gaps behind the rival average.
4. For each weak pillar, summarise the review themes in your own words (2–3 themes each).

OUTPUT
- Bottom line: 2 sentences — where [Company] trails its hiring rivals and the RPO angle that follows.
- Header: [Company], overall index, reviews analysed, scope (company-wide or [Location]).
- Table: Pillar | [Company] | each rival | Rival average | Gap. Worst gap first.
- "Weakest 3": Pillar | Score | Gap | What employees say (themes).
- "The RPO angle": per weak pillar, one line on how [What I sell] would help (candidate experience, employer messaging, sourcing reach, offer competitiveness).
- Recommended next step: an opening line for the head of talent acquisition, framed around one gap against a named rival, and why now.
- Gaps: what Draup didn't have — worth asking in discovery.

RULES
- Mark any company with fewer than 200 reviews analysed as low confidence (editable default), and don't build the opening line on it.
- Paraphrase review themes. Never quote or identify individual reviewers.
- Keep the tone constructive: frame gaps as opportunities, since this may reach the client.

STANDARD RULES (leave as is)
- If an input still shows its bracketed example, use my saved context or ask me before starting.
- Date every number and fact. If Draup has no data, write "Not in Draup"; never fill gaps from memory.
- If the Draup for Talent connector is missing or returns an access error, stop and tell me; never estimate from memory.

followups: Show how hard it is for [Company] to hire its top 3 roles in [Location]. || Turn this into a 5-slide outline for an RPO discovery meeting. || Which pillar is [Company] strongest on, so we can acknowledge it first?
